hints: Look at conductivity first, it is the fastest way to tell ionic, metallic, simple covalent and giant covalent apart.
W conducts when liquid and in water but not as a solid, so it must be ionic with mobile ions only after melting or dissolving.
Check melting points to finish the job, a very high melting metal like iron fits Y, and a non-conducting giant solid fits Z.
walkthrough:
**Identify W as an ionic compound**

W has a high melting point, does not conduct as a solid, but conducts well as a liquid and in water. That is classic ionic behaviour. Ions are locked in the lattice when solid, but free to move when molten or in solution.

Rule: ionic solid = poor conductor, ionic liquid or aqueous = good conductor

**Identify X as a simple covalent liquid**

X has a very low melting point of $-119^{\circ}\text{C}$ and boiling point of $39^{\circ}\text{C}$, and never conducts. That means weak intermolecular forces and no mobile ions or electrons, so simple molecular covalent. It is also insoluble in water.

This fits $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ (bromoethane), not $\text{HCl}$ which dissolves to give conducting $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions.

**Identify Y as a metal**

Y conducts well as both solid and liquid, and is insoluble in water. Only metals have a sea of delocalised electrons that conduct in both states. Its melting point is $1535^{\circ}\text{C}$.

This matches $\text{Fe}$ (iron, mp about $1538^{\circ}\text{C}$), not $\text{K}$ (potassium, mp only about $63^{\circ}\text{C}$).

**Identify Z as a giant covalent solid**

Z has very high melting and boiling points but never conducts in any state. That means a giant network of strong covalent bonds with no free ions or electrons.

This matches $\text{SiO}_2$ (silicon dioxide). $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is largely ionic and would conduct when molten, so it is ruled out.

**Choose the matching row**

W is an ionic solid with mp $993^{\circ}\text{C}$, which fits $\text{NaF}$ much better than $\text{MgO}$ ($\text{MgO}$ melts above $2800^{\circ}\text{C}$ due to $2+$ and $2-$ charges). So W = $\text{NaF}$, X = $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$, Y = $\text{Fe}$, Z = $\text{SiO}_2$.

options.A: W cannot be MgO because MgO has doubly charged ions ($\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{O}^{2-}$) and a melting point over $2800^{\circ}\text{C}$, far above 993. Z cannot be $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ because molten aluminium oxide contains mobile ions and conducts, but Z never conducts.
options.B: W is not MgO for the same high lattice energy reason, X is not HCl because HCl is very soluble and gives a conducting solution in water, Y is not K because K melts near $63^{\circ}\text{C}$, not $1535^{\circ}\text{C}$, and Z is not $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ as it would conduct when molten.
options.C: This row fits perfectly. NaF is ionic with mp near $993^{\circ}\text{C}$ and conducts when molten or aqueous. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ is simple covalent, low mp and bp, non-conducting and insoluble. Fe is metallic, conducting in solid and liquid with mp $1535^{\circ}\text{C}$. $\text{SiO}_2$ is giant covalent, very high mp, never conducting.
options.D: Although W = NaF and Z = $\text{SiO}_2$ are correct types, X cannot be HCl because X is insoluble and non-conducting in water, while HCl forms conducting hydrochloric acid. Y cannot be K because K is a soft low-melting metal, not a $1535^{\circ}\text{C}$ metal like Fe.
